265.title: Tita and La Cueva del Zoncho
265.excerpt: Everyone who has been to La Cueva del Zoncho in Santa María de Dota knows this magical place is what it is thanks to an inspiring woman who decided to make La Cueva more than her home, turning it into a space filled with history, art, and culture built over three decades.
265.content:
Everyone who has been to La Cueva del Zoncho in Santa María de Dota knows this magical place is what it is thanks to an inspiring woman who decided to make La Cueva more than her home, turning it into a space filled with history, art, and culture that
has been built over three decades.

We are talking about Flor Emilia Ureña, better known as Tita, whom we drew away from her routine to chat and learn more about her life. Naturally, she welcomed us with a smile and a long, colorful dress, two of her trademarks.

Nearly 66 years ago, Tita was born in an adobe house in Santa María, as she explains when we ask about her childhood:

“I think my childhood was the most beautiful, and my life has been very lovely. We were free back then: no cell phones, no cars, no electricity. My childhood was very different from yours. I consider myself a happy person. Like anyone, things happen, you feel down and try to get back up, but I have lived very, very well in this town.”

Tita tells us that loquats, jocotes, lemons, and oranges are her favorite fruits because of the beautiful childhood memories they bring back. The pandemic allowed her to recreate those moments:

“During the pandemic, I said, ‘The business is closed, so I am going to do what I used to!’ I went to my siblings’ farms to pick mangoes and loquats, and every day I ate fruit like when I was little. I daydreamed and relived my childhood. That was how it was: you left home after some aguadulce and a piece of bread and went to play all over town, eating guavas, loquats, and jocotes.”

Tita says her parents taught her to work from the age of five. She is deeply grateful for that because it allowed her to build what she has today through hard work and enjoy unique experiences she never imagined, such as living in Panama for ten years.

“In Panama, after the invasion, I moved to one of the most troubled neighborhoods. I lived there and saw so much from my balcony that I also learned not to judge people, because I imagined what it would have been like to be born there, where women carried a knife behind their backs and children were made to sell drugs. I think those experiences helped me run this place, La Cueva.”

She has been in charge of La Cueva, her business and home, for 33 years, since her father died. She told us he built it between 1967 and 1969 from a very old adobe house, adding a room at the back to use as a dance hall.

“People had already called this place La Cueva, because a man nicknamed ‘Pata e’zoncho’ helped my dad build it. People came and said, ‘Look, this is the vulture’s cave!’ And the name stuck.”

But what, according to Tita, makes La Cueva so beloved by so many people and generations from Los Santos and beyond?

“Because I live here, my motto has always been that everyone is welcome in my home and should feel at home, knowing I am someone who will not judge anyone. Bohemians from around the world come here; everyone has a story and a life. The people who come here are intelligent. Some people have become angry because I want to make room for everyone, but I tell them this is how La Cueva is. If they want to come, they can, but I am not changing the rules.”

There are clearly defined rules at La Cueva, and they are strictly enforced. Some are:

  • Anyone can enter La Cueva.
  • Anyone who fights gets water thrown on them.
  • Anyone who sells drugs is banned from returning.
  • People who use drugs are not allowed to use them inside La Cueva.
 

“I believe every place has its charm and energy if you experience it with passion.”

Those of us who live in Los Santos see every summer how La Cueva welcomes hundreds of Indigenous and Nicaraguan people who come to work in the coffee harvest. But why has Tita opened her door to these communities, who often face rejection elsewhere?

“I always heard how Nicaraguan and Indigenous people were treated. I did not know much about their cultures, but I became very interested in learning. I asked them to take me traveling, and that is why I have made fourteen trips to Nicaragua, to many marginalized areas. People asked why I went to those neighborhoods if they were dangerous, but because I went with an energy of love, God always protects you. I learned so much about their culture there, and I love their food. They are very humble people; many live in remote rural areas, and they are not bad people. I think that if reincarnation exists, in a past life I was Nicaraguan or Indigenous.”

Tita’s many trips to Nicaragua are a small part of her travels across the 28 countries she has visited. She has returned to some more than once, including Guatemala, which she has visited thirteen times, and Panama, which she still visits frequently.

All these experiences emerge in conversation with Tita, making the value culture brings to people’s lives clear to anyone.

“When you get to know other cultures, you can consider what is right or wrong for each of them. It is better to visit each place, adapt, and show respect. That is what you learn most: respect.”

Tita has always been open to every form of cultural and artistic expression. That is why she has turned La Cueva into a nationally recognized stage that has welcomed hundreds of musicians over the years, even helping launch dozens of local bands that took their first steps there.

“I had seen rock bands at big fairs in other countries, and those beautiful concerts gave me goosebumps. What a beautiful thing! I would say, ‘How lovely if they came to La Cueva one day!’ But I did not have the space or capacity for groups like that. In those years, young people from town came to tell me they had instruments and music and wanted to put on a concert here. I said, ‘Of course, come!’ Sometimes I hid because it sounded awful and I felt embarrassed, but we had to encourage and support them. If someone ever objects to concerts in my business, fine, but I can die in peace because we have already broken down that idea of ‘singing to the devil.’ We are becoming more aware, because that came from a lack of education.”

Tita tells us it is very important to keep creating new places in the region and organizing artistic activities for children, young people, and adults, to encourage and educate the community through art. She assures us La Cueva will always be available to anyone wanting to make music, put on theater, hold reading circles, play board games, or organize any other activity. That is what La Cueva del Zoncho is for: going there and enjoying it.

For the Santos Rock Cultural Association, Tita’s energy and support have been vital to our collective’s development. She joins our activities, advises us, and always opens her doors to diverse cultural events and spaces. We believe Tita deserves every recognition from Los Santos for promoting local culture for decades. We hope more and more people make La Cueva their home and a place to meet, have fun, and gather, just as she has always wanted.

1814.title: Fuerza Dread at Santos Rock 2025: Commitment, emotion, and roots reggae
1814.excerpt: At the ninth Santos Rock festival in 2025, held at Rancho Turístico El Guayabal, Fuerza Dread’s appearance was one of the event’s most moving moments. The band from Puntarenas, with nearly two decades of experience, performed its signature roots reggae blended with funk, jazz, and rock.
1814.content:
At the ninth Santos Rock festival in 2025, held at Rancho Turístico El Guayabal, Fuerza Dread’s appearance was one of the event’s most moving moments. The band from Puntarenas, with nearly two decades of experience, performed its signature roots reggae blended with funk, jazz, and rock.

We had the opportunity to speak with the members at Cafetería Coopedota, one of the event’s official sponsors, where they shared their impressions of the festival and the emotional bond they formed with the audience.

“Without a doubt, the people… hearing everyone sing the songs… it actually gave me goosebumps.”

The band described the experience as a moment that reaffirmed their commitment to music and to the project they have been building for years. “It makes us feel very committed to the project and the work we are doing,” they said. 

They also shared their joy at the festival’s diverse lineup, where ska, metal, reggae, and rock came together in a single day. “There was a little bit of everything,” they said, appreciating the range of musical approaches that enrich the national scene.

Another highlight was the opportunity to play outside the Central Valley and the pleasant surprise it brought:

“Sometimes you have this idea that the whole scene happens in the Central Valley… but arriving and receiving that warmth here in Dota… it was incredible.”

Finally, they shared a message for those starting out in music: “Fear will always be part of any process… but if we turn that fear into an ‘I can,’ that is where everything begins.”

Fuerza Dread delivered a memorable show at Santos Rock 2025 and reaffirmed that its place in Costa Rican music is built on authenticity, consistent work, and the positive message it conveys through every note.

Here is the interview on our official Instagram.

1844.title: Rana Bruja: Magic, energy, and surf on the Santos Rock 2025 stage
1844.excerpt: Rana Bruja’s second appearance at Santos Rock, in 2025, was incredible. From the moment they took the stage, the audience responded energetically to this band made up mostly of women.
1844.content:
Rana Bruja’s second appearance at Santos Rock, in 2025, was incredible. From the moment they took the stage, the audience responded energetically to this band made up mostly of women.

Formed in 2020 during the pandemic, Rana Bruja quickly established itself as a fresh presence on the scene, blending surf rock with a touch of post-punk. 

“The festival atmosphere has been really awesome for us because there have been so many bands. It has been impressive, and people have honestly been dancing the whole time… I have enjoyed it so much,” said Sol, highlighting the audience’s connection with every band. 

One of their show’s most memorable moments was playing “La Cacería,” a song the band has recently reinvented. “People were singing it… for me, that was incredible.”

“We love collaborating… the energy Free brings to the stage is really awesome too,” said the band’s drummer, Eva Navarro.

Their message to anyone dreaming of starting a band was clear: “Go for it, it is really awesome. That is how we started… a message, and here we are.” They also emphasized taking the leap without fear: “Everyone starts from zero… you have to make mistakes to learn.”

With new songs on social media, Rana Bruja shows that the local scene is alive, diverse, and constantly growing. Their appearance at Santos Rock reaffirms their relevance and the need for events like this festival to give different musical voices a platform.

1859.title: Chemicide at Santos Rock 2025: Costa Rican thrash metal beyond borders
1859.excerpt: At the ninth Santos Rock festival in 2025, held at Rancho Turístico El Guayabal in Santa María de Dota, Costa Rican thrash metal band Chemicide delivered a performance the whole crowd enjoyed. Since beginning in 2008, Chemicide has established its presence on the international metal scene.
1859.content:
At the ninth Santos Rock festival in 2025, held at Rancho Turístico El Guayabal in Santa María de Dota, Costa Rican thrash metal band Chemicide delivered a performance the whole crowd enjoyed. Since beginning in 2008, Chemicide has established its presence on the international metal scene. 

In an interview after their concert, guitarist and vocalist Frankie shared his impressions of the festival and the connection with the audience:

“The atmosphere here at Santos Rock is honestly awesome… the audience was really into it.”

Chemicide has shown that perseverance is key in music. Frankie reflected on the challenges facing emerging musicians:

“I think obsession beats talent… there are so many better musicians… who perhaps cannot handle the constant rejection you face.”

The band recently released its fifth studio album, “Violence Prevails,” on February 28, 2025 through French label Listenable Records. Featuring tracks such as “Red Giant,” the album has been well received by critics and shows Chemicide’s musical evolution.

By taking part in Santos Rock 2025, Chemicide reaffirms its commitment to Costa Rican music and its ability to connect with local and international audiences. Their festival appearance stood out for its musical quality and for the message of perseverance and authenticity they convey through their art.

1880.title: Ominosa returns in force at Santos Rock 2025: Reuniting with the Los Santos metal community
1880.excerpt: Costa Rican band Ominosa shared its music after returning from a break of several years. Formed in 2017 in Los Santos, Ominosa is known for its progressive death metal style.
1880.content:
At the ninth Santos Rock festival in 2025, held at Rancho Turístico El Guayabal in Santa María de Dota, Costa Rican band Ominosa shared its music after returning from a break of several years. Formed in 2017 in Los Santos, Ominosa is known for its progressive death metal style.

During their performance, the band played songs such as “From Skies Above,” which resonated deeply with the audience. The track, from their self-titled EP released in 2018, reflects Ominosa’s musical evolution and commitment to Costa Rican metal. 

In an interview, Ominosa shared their impressions of the festival and the importance of community in music:

“So many bands come together here. We reunite with friends we have not seen in years and with those who always support us. The experience is always really pleasant; as Gabo says, we are a community. Everyone supports each other here, among the bands and the audience too.”

The band also highlighted the crowd’s energy during their performance:

“A memorable part was the last song, ‘From Skies Above.’ I wanted people to join in with some backing vocals, and it worked. That had never happened before: a band opening Santos Rock and making that connection.”

Ominosa has shown that music is a powerful tool for expression and personal growth. Their return to Santos Rock 2025 reaffirms their place in Costa Rican metal and inspires new generations to find in music a way to face and overcome life’s challenges.

1924.title: Overshock at Santos Rock 2025: Moshing, energy, and connection with the crowd
1924.excerpt:
From the start of their performance, Overshock showed their potential within Costa Rican metal. Santos Rock 2025 marked a very important moment for the band:
“This is really the first time we have played in front of so many people,” they shared after their performance.
1924.content:
From the start of their performance, Overshock showed their potential within Costa Rican metal. Santos Rock 2025 marked a very important moment for the band:
“This is really the first time we have played in front of so many people,” they shared after their performance. According to the band, the festival’s atmosphere reflected the spirit that defines Los Santos: diversity, openness, and energy. 

“You can tell people are eager to see bands, regardless of genre. I love that, because you reach people who would not normally come to one of your shows,” they said, highlighting how these events allow artists and listeners to discover each other.

One of the most intense moments came when they played “Breathe.” During the breakdown, the crowd started moshing, reaffirming the unique connection between stage and audience.
“Seeing everyone join the mosh… it is a back-and-forth that feels really beautiful.”

When speaking to younger generations, Overshock has no doubts: you have to go for it.
“We could say we are part of the new generation too… you have to go for it without fear, practice, and enjoy it, because dreams do come true.”

Overshock brought power to the stage and a clear message: music is about connection, passion, and community.

1938.title: Puerko Xpin: The return of a local legend.
1938.excerpt: With thirteen years of history and a long-awaited comeback, Puerko Xpin lit up the Santos Rock stage again with an energy that can only come from a deep connection with the community where they began. “We are Puerko Xpin,” they announced forcefully, reaffirming their place as an iconic band from Los Santos.
1938.content:
With thirteen years of history and a long-awaited comeback, Puerko Xpin lit up the Santos Rock stage again with an energy that can only come from a deep connection with the community where they began. “We are Puerko Xpin,” they announced forcefully, reaffirming their place as an iconic band from Los Santos.

According to the band, the festival’s atmosphere has evolved. Today it is a meeting point for bands of different genres and a place where art flourishes in all its forms, with a special place for families.

“It is a family atmosphere, a space to create art; there are more than just bands,” they say proudly.

One of the most memorable moments of their performance featured Alina and Dalí, two girls in the audience who began dancing in the circle. “That shows the family atmosphere and the respect,” they said, visibly moved.

The scene captured what Santos Rock means: music, community, and generations sharing the same rhythm.

Puerko Xpin reminds new bands of its own beginnings: “We started very young, without instruments, always borrowing them.”

Their advice is clear: “Do not back down, even though there are always obstacles. Do not let it die. There will always be people who support you.”

Santos Rock 2025 witnessed the rebirth of Puerko Xpin, a band that shows how passion for music and mutual support can sustain a dream for more than a decade.

1970.title: Overseas at Santos Rock 2025: Community, diversity, and moshing as therapy
1970.excerpt:
With more than 20 years on the Costa Rican punk scene, Overseas arrived at Santos Rock 2025 with a blend of energy and connection with the audience.

“The atmosphere here is honestly really cool.”
1970.content:
With more than 20 years on the Costa Rican punk scene, Overseas arrived at Santos Rock 2025 with a blend of energy and connection with the audience. “The atmosphere here is honestly really cool.”

After their set, the band was excited about the warmth of the festival audience. They also emphasized the importance of taking part in an event that contributes to the region’s culture, highlighting the value of places like this for sharing music and art in general. 

Among the things they valued most were the festival’s mix of genres and the mutual respect between bands and attendees: 

“It is really awesome to see the audience connect with all the bands at such a varied festival, even when they play different genres,” they said.

For them, diversity is one of the event’s greatest strengths.

The most memorable moment came when the audience formed a mosh pit during their performance. “Seeing people who knew our songs, seeing the mosh pit get intense… people having a good time. That was a big highlight of the week.”

Overseas also spoke about the impact of Los Santos’ beauty: “The scenery is gorgeous… we arrived at sunset, and the sunlight looked beautiful on the mountains.” 

For the band, the surroundings enrich the festival’s cultural and travel experience. Their interview ended with a direct message to those starting out in music: “Even if you sometimes feel like throwing in the towel, if you really love this, keep fighting for it… if you have the chance to keep doing this as adults, make the most of it.”

Overseas brought punk to the stage, along with a lesson in perseverance and love for music.

1980.title: Alphabetics at Santos Rock 2025: An honest and explosive debut in Los Santos
1980.excerpt:
After more than a decade on the Costa Rican music scene, Alphabetics finally made its first appearance in Los Santos at Santos Rock 2025, with a show full of energy, emotion, and connection with the audience.

“It has been incredible; the people are so warm, everyone has such great energy.”
1980.content:
With more than a decade on the Costa Rican music scene, Alphabetics finally made its first appearance in Los Santos at Santos Rock 2025, with a show full of energy, emotion, and connection with the audience. “It has been incredible; the people are so warm, everyone has such great energy.”

They said this after their show, highlighting the warmth of an audience that knew their songs and sang them with real heart. They described the crowd as the festival’s most memorable part, particularly its “super explosive” response, in their own words.

Despite their established career, Alphabetics had never played in Los Santos before. They told us: “We only made it out here today, and it finally happened… honestly, the people are so awesome.”

This first visit to the region became a celebration for the band and its audience. Alongside their live performance, the band took the opportunity to share a powerful message with emerging musicians: 

“Be yourselves. It is lovely to have influences, but there is nothing more beautiful than hearing music that speaks for you.”

2002.title: No Apto Para Consumo at Santos Rock 2025: Punk, passion, and voices in unison
2002.excerpt: Since forming, No Apto Para Consumo has established itself as a representative band of Costa Rican punk, blending ska and rock to create a unique sound. Powerful lyrics and live energy that connects deeply with audiences have defined its presence on the national music scene.
2002.content:
Since forming, No Apto Para Consumo has established itself as a representative band of Costa Rican punk, blending ska and rock to create a unique sound. Powerful lyrics and live energy that connects deeply with audiences have defined its presence on the national music scene. 

We welcomed them to the stage at the last Santos Rock, in a memorable performance for both the audience and the band. Excited by the crowd’s response, they told us: 

“The atmosphere was honestly everything we had hoped for and more.” 

For No Apto Para Consumo, one of the festival’s most memorable moments was performing “Fugitivo,” when the crowd sang together, creating an incredible atmosphere: 

 “For me, it was a magical moment… seeing everyone sing with one voice.” 

Beyond the music, No Apto Para Consumo delivered a powerful message to younger generations: “It is so important for young people to feel motivated… this comes from the heart.”

Their appearance reaffirmed their commitment to music and their desire to inspire others to follow their passions. As a young band from Los Santos, their lyrics and stage presence give us so much inspiration.

2041.title: Santo Remedio at Santos Rock 2025: Music with soul and family connection
2041.excerpt: Since forming in 2017 in the Los Santos region of San José, Costa Rica, Santo Remedio has blended genres such as ska, cumbia, reggae, and Latin rock, creating an authentic sound.
2041.content:
Since forming in 2017 in the Los Santos region of San José, Costa Rica, Santo Remedio has blended genres such as ska, cumbia, reggae, and Latin rock, creating an authentic sound.

At Santos Rock 2025, Santo Remedio highlighted the importance of places where families can enjoy music outdoors. They told us: 

“It is lovely to see that people have a place to come with their families, where everyone can enjoy a concert.” 

For the band, the most special moments of playing live involve the audience. Santo Remedio emphasizes the joy of hearing people sing their songs wholeheartedly: 

“It feels so wonderful to play while people sing and to connect with the audience,” they said, emphasizing their emotional bond with the people of the region.

Santo Remedio also shared a message for emerging musicians: the importance of consistency and perseverance. 

“Be consistent, persistent… you have to be stubborn and keep going,” they advised, encouraging artists to trust their path and keep their passion for music alive.

Through their participation in Santos Rock 2025, Santo Remedio reminds us of the importance of perseverance.

Santo Remedio filled the Santos Rock 2025 stage with rhythm and made it clear that music can also be a refuge, a family, and a conviction. Their appearance was a celebration of authenticity, a reminder that sharing what you love remains the best remedy.

2137.title: Artists from Los Santos represent Costa Rica on an international album for Palestine
2137.excerpt: Three Costa Rican artists from the Los Santos region—Jenny Abarca, rapper Dopa G, and Chejo G—are taking part in the international album “Palestina Libre,” a musical project against genocide and in defense of human rights, bringing together 50 artists from 13 countries in a collaborative collection of 40 songs for freedom and peace.
2137.content:
Three Costa Rican artists from the Los Santos region—Jenny Abarca, rapper Dopa G, and Chejo G—are taking part in the international album “Palestina Libre,” a musical project against genocide and in defense of human rights, bringing together 50 artists from 13 countries in a collaborative collection of 40 songs for freedom and peace.

The album, officially released on August 15, 2025 on all digital platforms, is an expression of art and activism in which music becomes a tool for speaking out, resistance, and hope

Costa Rica brings its own voice

Costa Rica’s contribution to the album is a song written by Jenny Abarca together with Chejo G and Dopa G, carrying a powerful message from the mountains of Los Santos to listeners around the world.

“We joined this project from the heart, convinced that art can break down borders, denounce injustice, and build bridges of solidarity,” said Jenny Abarca.

The three artists bring an authentic perspective rooted in their regional identity, adding their talent to a cause that demands international justice and peace for the Palestinian people.

A project with global reach

Palestina Libre began as an initiative by Spanish musicians José Riaza and Eloy Acosta, who mobilized the international artistic community to create a collective album in response to the cruelty of genocide. The production has the support of the NGO Más Música, Menos Balas and the record label SocSub (Sociedad Subterránea).

Alongside the album, launch concerts, audiovisual showcases, and art exhibitions will take place in different countries, with active participation from the musicians involved.

2457.title: A festival twenty years later: A personal history of Santos Rock
2457.excerpt: That afternoon we were in San Pablo when the police stopped us and took us to the station. Jonathan, Luis, and me. Jonathan and I had taken a local bus from Santa María. We stopped in San Marcos, where Luis joined us. I was carrying a jar of starch paste my mom had helped me make. Jonathan had a bag of printed festival posters.
2457.content:
That afternoon we were in San Pablo when the police stopped us and took us to the station. Jonathan, Luis, and me. Jonathan and I had taken a local bus from Santa María. We stopped in San Marcos, where Luis joined us. I was carrying a jar of starch paste my mom had helped me make. Jonathan had a bag of printed festival posters.

It was late in the year. This was the second Santos Rock festival. We were kids—I was about to turn seventeen—and there at the station, Jonathan and I had no idea what to do. Luis did: he asked for the phone and called a friend of his dad’s who was a lawyer. They let us go immediately.

I had learned something a year earlier. Putting on a festival almost alone, with no experience, is a very effective form of torture. Even so, a year later I wanted to do it again, though with less pain and frustration this time. From the outset, I knew it would be best to involve more people. Many friends had seen what happened in 2006 and joined in.

Nanú and I had pushed the first festival forward, with occasional help from other friends before and after the event. Nothing systematic. But what happened at that first edition sparked enthusiasm in many more people. It showed us that a music festival in those little Los Santos towns really had potential. We had to keep going. Even if we screwed up. Screwed up again. Screwed up better.

A regional music scene

My cousin Mela had taken over as president of the Cantonal Young Persons Committee during that period. When she arrived, she found a surplus of unspent money. Although she already had some ideas about what to do with it, she asked me what else I could think of.

At the time, I was really into music magazines—especially the ones that reached Costa Rica from Spain at least six months late. Those magazines often reviewed Europe’s summer festivals. Lots of bands, sound and lights, people and beer. That combination of elements—and here is the key—came together outdoors, with sunshine and mountains.

Meanwhile, the first Costa Rock had taken place in late 2006, organized by Giovanny Durán of El Guato. The festival brought together thirty-three Costa Rican pop, rock, metal, punk, ska, and reggae bands in an event that started at noon and ended at midnight. Although I was a fifteen-year-old kid, I managed to pass my enthusiasm on to a responsible adult—meaning my older brother, René.

René had the idea of renting a minibus for about ten people, buying ten festival tickets, and advertising a package with admission and round-trip travel from Los Santos. That was how I started pasting posters on utility poles. We gathered ten people and headed to Paraíso de Cartago at the end of October.

For a kid like me, drinking in “Costa Rican rock” from the inexhaustible source that was Radio U—especially shows such as Punto de Garaje—going to that festival was a revelation. I saw many bands I loved; the Hormigas en la Pared performance is burned into my memory. Many of us also discovered bands just starting to become known, such as Los Cuchillos, who had appeared on the scene a year earlier.

With that recent Costa Rock experience in mind, alongside the collection of magazines piling up in my room, full of photographs of festivals surrounded by mountains, I had an idea that I shared with Melania. I probably said something like: “Mela, what if we used the committee’s money to put on a music festival at El Guayabal?”

El Guayabal was already well known in the region. It hosted interschool dances. In the pasture and small wood surrounding the hall, plenty of people had their first kisses and received a few anatomy lessons. At the time, it also still hosted livestock fairs, which drew far more than cattle experts: people from all three Los Santos cantons came for the dances, ranchera and tropical music concerts, saturated fats, and alcohol.

I knew immediately that the place was perfect for a music festival. We certainly never aspired to draw the crowds that attended the livestock fairs, but we could trust that a good number of people would come. Especially because, thanks to the Young Persons Committee’s funding, the first festival was free. Above all, though, what we wanted to highlight—or the festival’s goal, really—was that it could be sustained mainly by local bands from the three Los Santos cantons and neighboring towns in southern San José and Cartago. These local bands would also share the stage with bands from the “national scene” that we liked and admired. 

A year earlier—in 2005—I had attended a concert at La Cueva. Rock of Tarrazú read the poster I came across one afternoon on my way home from school. Seeing that poster, printed on red paper, was how I first learned that the neighboring canton had a music scene. [For the record: that show was when I discovered the Tarrazú scene, but it had already been active for many years.]

The concert would be at La Cueva in Santa María de Dota, just a few meters from home. I did what I needed to get my mom’s permission and went. Manrique Sánchez must have organized it; he was very active in several music projects and in organizing shows at the time. I do not remember exactly which bands played. I do remember Sobredosis, one of my favorite Los Santos bands. Punto de Partida and Pandemia—Manrique’s project back then—probably played too, and perhaps one of the many bands Pablo Zúñiga has put together. I think he was flirting with black metal and goth at the time and had formed a band called Sontuniversia.

That fortunate convergence let us move from idea to action. I was discovering that music festivals were important events in Costa Rica’s music scene. I could see that our town had suitable spots for putting one together. At the same time, I could see a music scene forming that was already moving beyond the cantons’ narrow geographical limits and the historic—and stupid—rivalries that made otherwise weak, insignificant borders seem so pronounced.

Back then, a thrash metal band called Equinoxis had formed at Dota’s high school. Its members came from Santa María and San Gerardo de Dota. Little by little, they also started getting together with bands from San Marcos. Rock was no longer music made only in Tarrazú. A regional scene was taking shape.

It is 2006, and the noise reaches El Guayabal

It must have been one of those Saturdays when Andrés and Michi, two musician friends from San Martín de León Cortés, would visit me to exchange music. I told them about the festival idea. At some point I also brought it to Nanú. Although I first put the idea into words with Michi and Andrés, it was with Nanú that the project got moving.

It may sound like a cliché. Stories are full of those pairings: Holmes and Watson, Batman and Robin, Pinky and the Brain. They all combine the same things. One embodies visionary madness, unrestrained impulse, imagination that overflows the bounds of good sense. The other contributes practical will and feet on the ground. While one invents the world, the other lives in it. That is what my friendship with Nanú has been like, and how I would describe the birth of Santos Rock. Madness needs willpower so it does not evaporate into pure fantasy, and willpower needs madness so it does not rot into mere routine.

People who know Nanú might say he embodies the madness in that equation, but at first it was the other way around. Nanú is about four years older than me. At the time, I was a timid, frightened minor. Nanú, meanwhile, had daring: he already had a license, drove “el Pichirilo”—his grandfather’s car—and possessed a wealth of practical knowledge that I, an inhabitant of my room’s bookish fantasy world, lacked. He took ownership of the idea and tackled many essential tasks that I could not or did not dare to undertake.

With Nanú as my partner and many other friends supporting us, things began moving. With Melania’s backing, we presented the project to the Cantonal Young Persons Committee, and our budget was approved. Having that money was a relief, and I still think it was more than that: it was a push forward, a way to see that the idea was possible. Being able to hire professional sound and cover many logistical expenses made us feel more secure. We began with greater confidence, putting together a call for bands, designing a poster in the most amateur way, and covering utility poles with starch paste.

That does not mean everything was simple. Again, we were teenagers with zero experience. Taking on tasks as we went, for which we were clearly unqualified, was a challenge. Picture that teenager shut in his room, trying to negotiate with a sound engineer who mentioned things called a “rider” or a “backline.” Those concepts were new and completely unfamiliar to me. I had to ask and learn.

Perhaps most importantly, many of our musician friends learned too. Once on the festival stage—or rather, the truck trailer serving as a stage—they discovered that stage monitors existed. These let them hear what they were playing instead of being drowned in noise and amplifier feedback. They learned to ask for “more gain” on their instruments, to use that equipment, and to try to sound better. Our learning was shared and collective.

But if navigating the preparations and reaching festival day in decent shape was difficult, the day itself revealed things we had not anticipated. The event had barely started when we discovered on the spot many other problems. Neither the bands nor we as organizers knew how to enforce a schedule or manage smooth transitions between performance times, running order, and downtime—while one band left the stage and another came on, soundchecked, and began playing. Many bands never arrived. Others arrived late. The closing band decided to play earlier so they could watch the national football match. It was a disastrous recipe for upsetting many musicians—with good reason—and sending me into crisis.

Again, we had to learn, take the knocks, and realize that this unwritten manual was really a living notebook of experiences. 

“We could quickly become frustrated, put our ambitions and projects away in a drawer, and each go our own way. Or we could pay attention to those experiences and do something with them, so we could continue with a better understanding of what we were doing.”

2007, a new edition: No money, but (some) experience

After seeing what was possible in 2006, we put together the second Santos Rock in December 2007. We no longer had funding, but we had learned something from the first festival. We decided we could manage it ourselves by holding a series of small concerts in local bars throughout the year, gradually raising money to finance the bigger event at year’s end.

There was Nanú, driving el Pichirilo everywhere, hauling Tito Zafiro’s amplifiers and drum kit. Friends and bands took part in those smaller events with a clear understanding: nobody kept the door money; it all went into a fund to be used entirely for Santos Rock. We called the concept “sábado acusticazo.” It generally used a smaller format with fewer technical requirements. The invitation and the formula worked, although the money was not enough.

When festival day arrived at the end of the year, some of us contributed from our thin student wallets and recovered the money at later concerts. What mattered was seeing that the project could exist without support from institutions or potential sponsors. Two things played important roles: first, the many more people who joined after seeing what happened in 2006; second, the availability of places tolerant of noise and lively young people passionate about music.

Talking about how this music scene developed in Los Santos means recognizing and thanking the willingness and support of people such as Tita and her daughter Xóchitl at “La Cueva”, and Tita’s brother, Jose Ureña, at El Guayabal. La Cueva bar in Santa María de Dota, and Tita’s openness to letting ska, punk, and even the most extreme metal bands make noise there, allowed this music scene to emerge, endure, and transform. Holding a festival like Santos Rock in 2007—again, without sponsors or any public or private institutional backing—was only possible because Tita and La Cueva were always willing to host the smaller concerts that financed the bigger event.

In fact, any music scene’s dependence on its venues explains why the festival reached an impasse after that second edition in 2007. The day before the event, many Santa María residents heard the priest’s sermon at Mass. He warned how inappropriate it was for that small town to give free rein to libertine, sinful activities such as a rock festival. The sermon worked. Our impression was that more people attended than the previous year. But the voices of disapproval, backed by the priest’s words, meant we lost the opportunity to repeat the festival at El Guayabal. Although we tried to find a new venue elsewhere in Los Santos, the search failed, and many of us became discouraged.

Ten years without Santos Rock (but with plenty happening)

In 2008, I was in eleventh grade. Although I kept looking for places to organize concerts and stay close to friends making music, things began changing for me and many of my friends. Some of us soon moved to San José and started university, while others began working. We only traveled back occasionally, and many of those new projects interrupted our musical ambitions.

That does not mean the Los Santos music scene died in those years. Many younger friends also started music projects, secured venues, created their own festivals, and undertook truly admirable efforts. That was how I met Gabo Montero, who began organizing metal shows and later joined Pablo Zúñiga in Istanbul, a project that brought sounds not very common in Los Santos at the time. The extreme metal scene was also very active, with bands such as Scars of Destruction, Suicidal Brain, and Dead Ivory. The latter included Andrey Araya, “Cabecita,” who had also belonged to the earlier generation from the early 2000s. Like Manrique Sánchez, Alejandro Vega “Tito,” Douglas Picado, and many others, he joined people starting bands in the early 2010s.

Alongside concerts at private parties, members of that incoming generation, such as Alex Jiménez and Edgar Muñoz with their Suicidal Brain bandmates, took the initiative to create events like Massacre Fest. Dedicated to metal, it began in 2011 and brought together Los Santos bands and nationally recognized acts. That same year, Gabo Montero and Luis Ricardo Castro, “Pizza,” founded Neurótica Producciones and began organizing many of the concerts held during that period.

That generational handover and continuity may have made it easier to consider reviving the festival ten years later. The circumstances were encouraging: many of us were returning to the region after finishing university. There was greater maturity—try not to fall over in surprise, eh!—and knowledge to take on a project like the festival again. Once more, the convergence of people from the early-2000s scene and those who had followed them proved essential.

There is also an emotional element worth mentioning. It was 2016. I was walking from San Pedro de Montes de Oca toward Curridabat when it hit me: that year marked ten years since the first festival. Nostalgia got the better of me. When I got home, I created a WhatsApp group, added the friends I knew might be up for it, and named it Santos Rock 2016.

It is January 2017, and we are back

I think Pablo Zúñiga was the first to reply, with surprised emojis (“😱😱😱😱”). I realized everyone I had added was excited by the idea. We began figuring out how to put everything together again. Some decisions were unavoidable, starting with whether to return to El Guayabal. We agreed to do so. But the dates of the towns’ traditional year-end patron saint festivities pushed us to hold the festival in January instead of December, as we had for the first two editions. We had also begun working late in the year, so aiming for the first month of the next year gave us more time to get organized.

The organizing group grew over time. I wanted to bring in the experience of those who had remained more active in the Los Santos scene while many of my friends and I had stepped away. Gabriel Montero was one of those additions, since Neurótica Producciones had been organizing events, particularly metal shows. Cristopher Barboza joined too, bringing experience with punk concerts. Many friends who had played in bands at the first Santos Rock festivals, participating more as musicians than organizers, now took on logistical tasks, including Pablo Zúñiga, Frin Durán, and “Josa” Porras.

Our combined contacts made it easier to build the lineup and hire sound, lighting, security, and the thousand other things these events always require. We started making noise as soon as we could, and excitement kept growing. Cris Barboza passed that enthusiasm on to his dad, and we soon added Anestesia Local to the lineup: the pioneering band that began playing rock in Tarrazú in the 1990s, with Luis Barboza, “Popocho”—Cris’s dad—singing alongside Canadian Bruce Callow.

Another example of generations coming together was Gargamel’s reunion. This pioneering band began playing punk in Tarrazú in the early 2000s. Two members, Fabián and Maikol Mora, had died in a tragic traffic accident descending the Abejonal in May 2006. Now, more than ten years later, Gargamel returned to the stage with Cris on drums and Pil on guitar: two members of PuerkoXpin, the punk band formed in 2011 and Gargamel’s undisputed successor.

We keep dancing, dreaming, singing (as Santo Remedio says)

That meeting of generations, which defined Santos Rock’s return, was fundamental. I would also say it has been the secret behind the festival’s continuity ever since. When preparations began for the edition following 2017, I decided to step aside and focus on my academic commitments. When I attended the January 2018 festival with friends from San José, I became convinced of something: I had conceived an idea, but it could continue perfectly well without me. The 2018 festival was excellent. My friends had secured a better stage, planned a lineup balanced across musical genres, delivered impeccable sound, and drawn a strong crowd

Although I rejoined the organizers the following year, I did so simply to help facilitate things. Besides organizing another festival, we tried to realize some earlier aspirations. We introduced a more professional graphic style and visual identity. We secured a Declaration of Cultural Interest from the Ministry of Culture and Youth, expanded media coverage, and obtained a good number of sponsors and institutional supporters. A documentary was filmed, briefly reviewing previous editions and taking stock of what had been achieved by 2019. We also established the Santos Rock Cultural Association, whose founding statutes identified its main purpose as “supporting, promoting, publicizing, and accompanying alternative artistic expressions arising in the particular context of the Los Santos region, especially musical initiatives related to rock and similar genres.”

In the middle of that year, I moved to Mexico City to study and live, building a life far removed from the Los Santos music scene that I care about so much. For that reason, I do not feel able to continue a first-person, openly testimonial account of a process in which I have not been directly involved. I would, however, like to consider how that distance allows me to address something relevant to understanding what continues to happen in the scene generally and at Santos Rock specifically.

The formation, development, and consolidation of a music scene depend on more than musicians, bands, and places to gather, drink beer, and make noise. They also need management, organization, and leadership. A scene can only endure and reinvent itself, however, when people hand over responsibility and leadership does not become entrenched. I can say confidently that this openness and reinvention have benefited Los Santos’ music scene. This may have led some people to distance themselves critically, which is entirely understandable and valid, especially when they feel that the way the festival is organized and its annual lineup have moved away from an ideal or from what worked before.

Beyond that nuance, it is worth observing how the cultural association, established in mid-2019 and now responsible for organizing the festival and other cultural events, has gained momentum and fresh energy through changes in leadership and the continual arrival of new members. That keeps the festival, and the wider scene, from becoming merely an anecdote. I would like to recognize and thank everyone involved in the association for their committed, professional work, particularly Jéssica and Javi, who have served as its presidents over these years.

That, I believe, is the main reason to celebrate twenty years of the idea and dream we had as kids pasting posters on utility poles. The first festival, born amid difficulties but with enormous enthusiasm, had a very clear goal. That idea remains the same today. It is also the glue joining the dedication, commitment, and spirit of the young people who now take our place.

The idea is that our friends’ and neighbors’ music has value, deserves to be shared in the best possible way, and has every merit needed to reach stages within and beyond our country. As long as people want to keep making noise, writing irreverent lyrics, gathering to start a mosh pit and celebrating friendship, that idea will remain alive.

Jesús Bedoya Ureña

Mexico City, Friday, October 10, 2025.

I thank Erandi Barroso for her attentive reading and valuable editorial comments. My thanks also go to Marco Méndez and Javier Solís for their observations, and to Pablo Zúñiga, Gabriel Montero, Álex Jiménez, and Cristopher Barboza for the information they provided.

2561.title: When the classroom becomes a stage: Zavaleta Music Fest 2025
2561.excerpt: On November 3, Colegio Técnico Profesional José Daniel Flores Zavaleta in Santa María de Dota enjoyed a day filled with music and community at the first Zavaleta Music Fest.
2561.content:
On November 3, Colegio Técnico Profesional José Daniel Flores Zavaleta in Santa María de Dota enjoyed a day filled with music and community at the first Zavaleta Music Fest. It was more than a concert: it was the culmination of an educational project in which art became a bridge between the classroom and the stage.

The idea did not begin as a formal festival:

“We thought of it as a classroom activity more than a festival. It is a project for tenth and eleventh graders. We did not just say: let’s put on a festival,” explained music teacher Heyner Rivera, the driving force behind the event.

What began as a classroom activity, with rehearsals and songs, grew as students made the project their own. Little by little, music became more than a subject: it became a source of creativity and collaboration. An academic activity turned into a community experience where everyone found a role, whether onstage or in logistics, decoration, or sound.

The students’ own enthusiasm transformed the idea into something much bigger. When they noticed that their work had an impact, that their classmates were joining in, and that the art they created moved other people, they stopped seeing it as an assignment and began experiencing it as a shared commitment.

The festival provided a platform for the school’s art and for the organizing talents of people who do not usually get involved in music.

“They gradually got involved, and when they saw how many people were signing up to help, they felt motivated and started bringing whatever was needed: decorations, this and that,” teacher Rivera recalls enthusiastically.

Performances ranged from Spanish-language rock classics such as Soda Stereo to more contemporary artists such as Mon Laferte and Carla Morrison. There was also room for guest artists and original compositions. The program had two blocks, with an intermission featuring food prepared by the school community.

For teacher Rivera, Zavaleta Music Fest is also an investment in local artistic identity:

“What I am exploring with the students is rock. I go in that direction because it is the root. After the root, you can move into other rhythms,” he explained, noting that rock represents the local musical output of the Los Santos region.

As part of their learning process, students researched the region’s music scene, from pioneering bands such as Anestesia Local to current names such as Santo Remedio and Rana Bruja.

“Ending with a concert is the practical side of all that knowledge,” the teacher said.

Advertising design students accompanied every performance through the lens of Zavaleta Studio, the school’s photography and video studio. Its team documented the entire event and captured the festival’s best moments. Thanks to their work, we can now relive the energy of the day. 

At Santos Rock, we warmly celebrate initiatives like this. Alongside talent, there is identity, collective work, and passion for what is ours. This new generation is arriving with strength and love for its music. We firmly believe they will take to the stages of the future and continue building our culture. 

To finish, here are some photographs and the event program.

3.title: Privacy policy
3.description: When visitors leave comments on the website, we collect the data shown in the comments form, as well as the visitor’s IP address and browser user agent string to help detect spam.

sections.7f8e7bb9:
Who we are

Our website address is: https://santosrock.com.

Comments

When visitors leave comments on the website, we collect the data shown in the comments form, as well as the visitor’s IP address and browser user agent string to help detect spam.

An anonymized string created from your email address (also called a hash) may be provided to the Gravatar service to see whether you are using it. The Gravatar service privacy policy is available here: https://automattic.com/privacy/. After your comment is approved, your profile picture is visible to the public in the context of your comment.

Media

If you upload images to the website, you should avoid uploading images with embedded location data (GPS EXIF). Visitors to the website can download and extract any location data from images on the website.

Cookies

If you leave a comment on our site, you may choose to save your name, email address, and website in cookies. These are for your convenience so that you do not have to fill in your details again when you leave another comment. These cookies will last for one year.

If you have an account and log in to this site, we will set a temporary cookie to determine whether your browser accepts cookies. This cookie contains no personal data and is discarded when you close your browser.

When you log in, we will also set several cookies to save your login information and screen display choices. Login cookies last for two days, and screen options cookies last for one year. If you select ‘Remember Me’, your login will persist for two weeks. If you log out of your account, the login cookies will be removed.

If you edit or publish an article, an additional cookie will be saved in your browser. This cookie contains no personal data and simply indicates the ID of the article you just edited. It expires after one day.

Embedded content from other websites

Articles on this site may include embedded content (for example, videos, images, articles, etc.). Embedded content from other websites behaves in exactly the same way as if the visitor had visited the other website.

These websites may collect data about you, use cookies, embed additional third-party tracking, and monitor your interaction with that embedded content, including tracking your interaction if you have an account and are logged in to that website.

Who we share your data with

If you request a password reset, your IP address will be included in the reset email.

How long we retain your data

If you leave a comment, the comment and its metadata are retained indefinitely. This allows us to recognize and approve follow-up comments automatically instead of holding them in a moderation queue.

For users who register on our website (if any), we also store the personal information they provide in their user profile. All users can view, edit, or delete their personal information at any time (except they cannot change their username). Website administrators can also view and edit that information.

What rights you have over your data

If you have an account or have left comments on this website, you can request an exported file of the personal data we hold about you, including any data you have provided. You can also request that we erase any personal data we hold about you. This does not include data we are required to retain for administrative, legal, or security purposes.

Where your data is sent

Visitor comments may be checked through an automated spam detection service.

sections.35305f0e:
About Santos Rock

The Santos Rock festival began through the efforts of a group of young people from the three cantons of the Los Santos region. The festival’s founders aimed to create spaces to promote and raise awareness of local bands playing rock and alternative music genres (metal, punk, ska, reggae, etc.).

The first edition of the event took place in 2006 with funding from the Cantonal Committee for Young People. Thanks to the support the festival received, a second, self-funded edition took place in 2007. After a nine-year break, the event returned as a commemorative edition. Strong support from audiences and artists encouraged the organizers to make Santos Rock an annual festival, a tradition that continues to this day.

In 2019, the Santos Rock Cultural Association was established to support, promote, share, and accompany alternative artistic expressions emerging in the Los Santos region. With this motivation, activities have been developed in collaboration with other cultural organizations in the region, encouraging and supporting artistic and cultural initiatives led by children and young people from the three cantons that make up the Los Santos region.

The festival thus provides a space where local bands can perform at a quality event with suitable conditions for promoting culture, encouraging artists to approach their projects professionally.

The Santos Rock Cultural Association provides musicians with all the technical, logistical, communication, and promotional resources they need, while strengthening relationships with established bands and musicians from the Costa Rican music scene. Together, these elements create an ideal setting for encouraging and reinforcing the efforts of local musicians.

sections.63989744:
frequently asked questions

How are bands selected for the Santos Rock Festival?

Bands for the Santos Rock Festival are selected during official meetings of the Cultural Association. Months before the event, we evaluate all the options, taking different factors into account, such as musical genre and the needs of the Los Santos audience.

As part of our commitment to the regional scene, we give priority to bands from Los Santos. However, we also consider bands from other parts of the country to provide a more musically enriching event. 

Our goal is to offer a variety of styles and genres to suit our audience’s tastes and create a diverse atmosphere at the festival.

How can I share my band’s material and information for the Santos Rock Festival selection process?

To share information about your band or project and take part in the selection process for the Santos Rock Festival, there are a few steps to keep in mind: 

  1. Send us an email at info@santosrock.com with your band’s information. Use the subject line ‘Participación Santos Rock’. 
  2. Include important details such as your name, biography, social media links, and links to your original music on streaming platforms, etc. 
  3. Also attach a press kit containing photos, interviews, concert posters, videos, links… The more information, the better! 
  4. It is also important to provide direct contact details (phone number and email address) with a reasonable response time so we can get in touch with you.
    We are thrilled that you would like to take part in the Festival! We look forward to receiving your material and learning more about your band. 

Do you have another question?
